newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary sees 1996 economic growth of 0.5 pct.
newsitem.headline: Hungary sees 1996 economic growth of 0.5 pct.

text.p: Hungary's gross domestic product (GDP) will probably grow by 0.5 percent this year while inflation should slow to 23 percent, a Finance Ministry official said on Wednesday.

The ministry also expects a 1996 current account deficit of less than $1.5 billion, smaller than earlier forecasts. The official said the volume of investments would show little change from the previous year, however.

Secretary of State Tibor Draskovics told a conference organised by the German-Hungarian Economic Chamber that Hungary has created the conditions necessary for economic growth and will keep its strict budgetary policies in 1997.
"The Hungarian economy can expect modest but well-supported economic growth in 1997," he said, adding that the GDP was likely to grow by two to three percent next year.
Hungary's fledgling market economy stabilised in the past two years after a slump that followed the collapse of the Comecon trading bloc in the early 1990s, Draskovics said.
Meanwhile, the role of the state in the economy has been reduced and government spending have been cut, he said.

As a result of economic austerity, real wages dropped some 15 percent in the past two years, but they are likely to stabilize in 1997, he said. Domestic consumption may even show modest growth in 1997.
Inflation was likely to drop to about 23 percent this year -- exceeding the 20 percent target -- and to 18 percent next year, he said.
However, the current account deficit will probably come in at $1.5 billion, well below the forecast $2 billion and the $2.5 billion deficit in 1995, he added.
Investments, which dropped in the first nine months, will pick up by the end of the year.
The improvement is expected to be driven partly by about 20 percent growth in processing, agriculture and housing construction, and a 40 percent increase in machinery industry exports, he said.
He added the government was determined to reduce its revenues and expenditures in 1997, begin the reform of the pension system and improve the profitability of enterprises.
The proportion of state redistribution to the GDP will drop to 47 to 48 percent in 1997 from 60 percent in 1994, Draskovics said.
The pension reform is expected to boost private funds, generating increased development sources of 30 to 40 billion forints for the economy by end of 1998, he added.
